nameStory: Water parsley gets its name from its deeply divided, serrated leaves that look remarkably similar to the parsley you might find in your kitchen garden. The "water" part reflects its love of wet places - you'll almost always find it growing along streams, in marshes, or even with its roots completely submerged in shallow water.
description: Water parsley is a tall perennial herb that can reach up to 5 feet in height, making it one of the more impressive members of the carrot family. Its large, bright green leaves are deeply divided into toothed leaflets that create a lacy, parsley-like appearance. The plant produces clusters of small white flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped heads typical of the carrot family. This western North American native is extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded sighting in the region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves up to 12 inches long with deeply divided, serrated leaflets that feel crisp and smell faintly celery-like when crushed. The leaf stalks can be even longer than the blades themselves, up to 14 inches.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers arranged in compound umbels - flat-topped clusters that look like tiny umbrellas. Some flowers may have a pinkish tinge, and the entire flower head can be 2-4 inches across.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright perennial that grows directly from wet soil or shallow water. Stems are hollow and feel somewhat succulent when squeezed gently.

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in or very near water - streambanks, marsh edges, or growing directly in shallow water with stems and lower leaves submerged.

habitat: In New England, water parsley would be found along streambanks, in freshwater marshes, or at pond edges where the soil stays consistently wet or waterlogged. It can grow as a true aquatic plant with its lower portions submerged in shallow water. Given its rarity here, any sighting would likely be near human settlements where it might have been introduced, rather than in remote natural areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the wet soil, with fresh green leaves unfurling. The distinctive parsley-like foliage becomes the main identifying feature as the plant begins its rapid upward growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with white umbrella-shaped flower clusters appearing at the top of tall stems. This is when the plant reaches its full impressive height and is most noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seeds develop. The large leaves may begin to yellow but often remain green well into autumn due to the consistently moist conditions.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the roots in New England's cold climate. Only dead stems may remain above ground, making identification impossible until spring regrowth.

funFact: Water parsley is such a successful colonizer that it went from zero known populations in Illinois to several thriving streamside colonies after just a single introduction, demonstrating how one escaped garden plant can completely change a local ecosystem within just a few years.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other members of the carrot family like wild parsnip or water hemlock, but water parsley's consistently wet habitat and extra-large, long-stalked leaves help distinguish it. Remember: if it's not growing in or right next to water, it's probably not water parsley.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, water parsley is not closely related to culinary parsley and should not be eaten. Like many members of the carrot family, proper identification is crucial since this family includes both edible plants and deadly poisonous ones like water hemlock.
compareHints: Water parsley is the only Oenanthe species reliably documented in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other large carrot family plants like wild parsnip or cow parsnip, water parsley's consistently aquatic habitat and extra-long leaf stalks make it distinctive. Its flowers are also typically smaller and more delicate than those of the robust upland carrot family species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Java water-dropwort differs from its relative water parsley by having more distinctly celery-like divided leaves rather than the broader, less-divided leaves of water parsley.
